questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/4f9f16654bc92f01c9cda8308ab4679695ed7d5055a12f6963303d4071c95bea.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/0234179c0a2dfb514a921f19e6fdc7bcad022aa0368d122a7d2ecc0e5d27df73.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=0$ and $y=2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={y}^{2}(2-y) \\ {y}^{′} & =y(2-y) \\ {y}^{′} & =y(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $y=0$ and $y=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<0$ | $0<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}(2-y).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}(2-y).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field by Identifying Asymptotic Behavior
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/660feebe44e179b53be85d23c497e58de4774258b588a6f8ac785a0fd9c8fc08.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2y-{y}^{2}-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{3}{y-1}$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/a76856ea0a6b50b821ba6c39e6a87a5acf5aabd704454b4875540b3970f3d249.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to 1.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are negative everywhere.

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2y-{y}^{2}-1}=-\frac{1}{(y-1)^{2}}
$$

gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to 1.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is negative for all $y\ne 1.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}=-\frac{y+1}{(1-\frac{1}{y})}\to ∓\infty \,\text{as}\,y\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{3}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are positive for $y>1.$

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=\pm 1.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y+1)(y-1)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =(y+1)(y-1) \\ {y}^{′} & =(y+1)^{2}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $y=\pm 1$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-1$ | $-1<y<1$ | $y>1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y+1)(y-1)^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y+1)(y-1)^{2}.$

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/ddac2bab6fb72979e1142179dfb11792cc50044de545131139edfdeff9215e3c.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope field is zero along the lines $y=\pm 2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on these lines.

Of the given equations, the only two that satisfy this condition are

$$
{y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}=(2+y)(2-y)
$$

 
and

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4=(y+2)(y-2).
$$

- Second, the lines $y=\pm 2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-2$ | $-2<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the two remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}=(2+y)(2-y).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field by Identifying Asymptotic Behavior
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/1a3ba94aa37bd8b8494794a7013956b100f418c9e0aa7efecab5ba6fc6476ff6.png)

Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/1a3ba94aa37bd8b8494794a7013956b100f418c9e0aa7efecab5ba6fc6476ff6.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes become vertical as $y\to \pm 1.$

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{(y+1)(y-1)} \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{1-{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{(1+y)(1-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become horizontal as $y\to 0.$

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}.
$$

Notice that

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}\to 0\,\text{as}\,y\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}$ become horizontal as $y\to 0.$

On the other hand,

$$
\frac{1}{1-{y}^{2}}\to 1\,\text{as}\,y\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{1-{y}^{2}}$ do *not* become horizontal as $y\to 0.$

So, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}.$
